explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Ruth 1:2 says the family "entered the land of Moab and settled there," so Moab is where they go. Ruth 1:1 says the same thing: they went "to reside in the land of Moab."
Egypt isn't where this family goes. Ruth 1:1 says they went to reside in the land of Moab, and Moab is the only new land named in the story. Keep Moab in your head for the rest of this passage.
Edom isn't in this passage at all. The text says the family settled in the land of Moab (Ruth 1:2). Moab is the answer here.
Ruth is the second name. Ruth 1:4 says the sons took Moabite women as their wives, "one named Orpah and the other named Ruth." That's the name that will matter most in this whole story.
Rachel isn't in Ruth 1 at all. The text names the two Moabite wives as Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Keep Rachel for another book, friend.
Dinah doesn't show up here. Ruth 1:4 gives the two names, and they are Orpah and Ruth. Dinah stays out of this family's story.
That's it, baker. Ruth 1:5 says "both Mahlon and Chilion also died," and Naomi "was left without her two sons and without her husband." Ten years in Moab and it all came apart.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: There's no fire in this passage. Ruth 1:5 tells us that Mahlon and Chilion died, and the house isn't mentioned at all. Stick with what the verse says.

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: Naomi doesn't lose her sight in this story. Ruth 1:5 says both of her sons died and she was left without her husband. Sickness and blindness aren't in the text.
Right, the LORD provided food for His people. Ruth 1:6 says Naomi "heard in Moab that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food." That news is what sends her home.
No king is named in this verse. Ruth 1:6 is about food, and the LORD providing it for His people. Keep your eyes on the bread, friend.
There's no battle in this verse, so victory isn't the news. Ruth 1:6 says the LORD had provided food for His people. Naomi hears about the food in Moab.

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: That's what Naomi says. Ruth 1:8 has her telling them, "Go back, each of you to your mother’s home." She sends them home to their own families, and that's the whole point of her speech.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse talks about speed or dark. Naomi's words in Ruth 1:8 are about going back to each mother's home. The road is only mentioned as the place they are walking.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: Naomi says the opposite of that. In Ruth 1:8 she tells them to go back to their mothers' homes. Staying close is what Ruth does later, not what Naomi asks for here.
True. Ruth 1:9 says, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband." Naomi is blessing both daughters-in-law, not just one.
The text says it is True. Naomi's blessing in Ruth 1:9 is for "each of you" to find rest in the home of a new husband. Both women are included.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Ruth 1:10 says, "Surely we will return with you to your people." They aren't ready to say goodbye to Naomi yet, and that's where they start.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: That's not what they say. In Ruth 1:10 the women answer Naomi, "Surely we will return with you to your people." Staying in Moab isn't in the text.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Visiting isn't mentioned here. Ruth 1:10 says they will return with Naomi to her people. The verse is about going with her, not a visit later.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: That's the question. Ruth 1:13 has Naomi asking, "would you wait for them to grow up?" She's laying out why the women should not stay tied to her and her sons.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Raising children isn't what Naomi asks. In Ruth 1:13 her question is whether they would wait for those sons to grow up. Keep that exact question in mind.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Going ahead to Bethlehem isn't in the question. Ruth 1:13 asks whether the women would wait for the sons to grow up. Bethlehem comes up in other verses, not this one.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: That's what Naomi says. In Ruth 1:13 she tells them, "it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." She feels the LORD's hand is the reason for her bitterness.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The people of Judah aren't named in this verse. Naomi says the LORD's hand has gone out against her (Ruth 1:13). Let's stick with what she says in the text.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: Nothing in Ruth 1:13 says the Moabites turned against her. Naomi names the LORD's hand as the reason for her bitterness. The verse doesn't go beyond that.
True. Ruth 1:14 says, "and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye." It's a sad goodbye, and that's the moment the story turns.
The text says it is True. In Ruth 1:14 Orpah kisses her mother-in-law goodbye. That's the part of the verse that goes with the weeping.
Not quite what happens. Ruth 1:14 says "but Ruth clung to her," meaning Ruth stays with Naomi. Orpah is the one who goes back.
That's right, baker. Ruth 1:14 says Ruth clung to Naomi, so she doesn't go home with Orpah. Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye, and Ruth stays.
True. Naomi says, "Look," and then, "your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home." That's the exact instruction Naomi gives Ruth in Ruth 1:15.
The text says it is True. In Ruth 1:15 Naomi tells Ruth to "follow her back home," meaning Orpah. Naomi is sending Ruth after Orpah.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: That's right. Ruth 1:16 has Ruth saying, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." She is promising to join Naomi's people and her God.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: Taking care of the house isn't in Ruth's words. In Ruth 1:16 she promises that "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." Stick with those two promises.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: Learning the ways of Judah isn't in the verse. Ruth 1:16 says "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." Those are her promises here.
That's the word. In Ruth 1:17 Ruth says, "if anything but death separates you and me." She's binding herself to Naomi, and only death is named as the thing that could separate them.
Distance isn't in that line. Ruth 1:17 says, "if anything but death separates you and me." Death is the one thing the verse names.
Marriage isn't in that line. Ruth 1:17 is about separation, and the only thing named there is death. Marriage doesn't come up in Ruth's oath.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: That's right. Ruth 1:18 says, "When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her." Naomi has finally seen Ruth's mind is made up.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: Naomi doesn't send Ruth back after Orpah in this verse. Ruth 1:18 says she stopped trying to persuade Ruth. The earlier verse was about following Orpah, but Ruth refused.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: Waiting in Moab isn't in the text. Ruth 1:18 says Naomi stopped trying to persuade Ruth once she saw Ruth was determined to go with her.
That's the line. Ruth 1:19 says the women of the town exclaimed, "Can this be Naomi?" The whole town is stirred, and that's the question they ask.
The women don't ask that. Ruth 1:19 has them exclaiming, "Can this be Naomi?" Naomi's husband is mentioned earlier, not in this question.
The women don't ask that. In Ruth 1:19 they ask, "Can this be Naomi?" Ruth is with her, but the question is about Naomi's identity.
That's right. Ruth 1:20 has Naomi saying, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me." She is asking them to use a new name because of her hard years.
Hannah isn't the name in this verse. Naomi says, "Call me Mara," in Ruth 1:20. That's the name she asks the women to use.
Leah doesn't come up here. Ruth 1:20 says Naomi asks them to call her Mara. Leah stays out of Ruth's story.
The text doesn't say that. In Ruth 1:21 Naomi says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty." She went away full and came back empty, not the other way around.
That's right, baker. Ruth 1:21 has Naomi saying, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty." She left full and came back empty, which is the reverse of what the card says.
Barley is the one. Ruth 1:22 says they arrived in Bethlehem "at the beginning of the barley harvest." The harvest is starting, and that's the setting for the next part of the story.
Wheat isn't named in this verse. Ruth 1:22 says they came at the beginning of the barley harvest. Keep barley in mind for this passage.
Olive isn't in the verse. Ruth 1:22 gives the harvest as barley, not olive. That's the word you want for this moment.
